Keep the brass archivist, but give it a job: it appears only in true empty states (no decks yet, no runs yet) with one line of copy, instead of being chrome on every page. That is where a mascot earns warmth rather than signalling a template.

sources_reviewed.name: Commander Spellbook (search results + combo detail + variants)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Its model keeps three things apart: the cards, what you need before you start, and what the combo produces. The Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring page is titled "Hullbreaker Horror | Sol Ring (and one other card)". It shows a template chip, "+ Permanent Castable for {C}", then Initial Card State ("in hand", "on the battlefield"), numbered Steps ("Repeat."), and Results ("Infinite colorless mana. Infinite storm count."). Metadata follows: "In 353140 decks according to EDHREC", a bracket tag ("Exhibition (Bracket 1+)") and a one-line reason ("No factors pushing this combo into a higher bracket were found"). A result is only called a win when it is one. Thassa's Oracle lines list "Win the game"; Hullbreaker + Sol Ring does not. Variants are grouped. The search has a "Variants grouped by combo: Yes/No" toggle and cards show "+ 29 variants". The detail page says "Below you find all 29 variants of this combo, with the alternative cards highlighted". Those 29 are the same Hullbreaker + Selvala loop with the third card swapped (Concordant Crossroads, Thousand-Year Elixir, Akroma's Memorial...). These are the exact cards behind Sim Lab's 28 near-duplicate Squirrel Girl rows.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A narrow search header, then a single column of result cards. Each card shows: colour identity line, "Cards in combo" list (names, with images on hover), a "+N other prerequisites" chip, a "Results in combo" list, and an EDHREC deck count. You can sort by popularity, price, number of variants, cards or results. The detail page puts a card image strip on top, then prerequisites, steps and results, then a metadata sidebar (bracket, colour identity, price, legality grid). A variants list sits at the bottom. Find My Combos splits results into "combos in your deck" and "combos needing one or more cards added", with bracket estimation on a separate tab.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Results read like a raw feature dump ("Infinite creature ETB, Infinite creature LTB, Infinite storm count"), which is jargon to casual players. Walls of near-identical cards appear if you turn variant grouping off. A cookie banner opens every visit. The steps assume you already know the stack.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This is the source Sim Lab's own combos.py reads, and its taxonomy already fixes the playtester's complaint. combos.py `_slim()` already keeps `produces` (the Results list) but drops the variant-to-combo relationship and the template or prerequisite pieces. Take: the results-based classification (win vs engine), variant grouping, the "+ template" chip, the bracket tag with its reason, and a deep link to each combo page. Avoid: re-explaining steps in Sim Lab. Link out instead, which also respects the don't-reimplement-Magic rule.

sources_reviewed.name: EDHREC (commander page + combos page)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Every number comes with its denominator. Card tiles read "47% inclusion / 4.04K decks of 8.66K decks / 38% synergy". Combo rows read "In 149759 decks (6.01% of 2492442)". Combos are summarised the way players talk about them: "2 card combo", "+1 other prerequisite", result chips ("Exile your library", "Win the game") truncated to "+3 more results", bracket dots 1 to 5, and "View combo details". It never calls an infinite-mana line a "win condition". A GC badge marks Game Changers inline next to card names ("Thassa's Oracle GC"). Theme tags with counts ("Spellslinger 879, Combo 271, Reanimator 200") tell you what a Kess deck is trying to do.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A hero strip holds the commander image, prices, rank and deck count. Below it are filter chips (Bracket 1 to 5, Budget, Tags), a tab row (Cards / Charts / Combos / Similar Commanders), and Group by / Sort by controls. The body is a responsive grid of card images grouped under headed sections (New Cards, High Synergy Cards, Top Cards, Game Changers, Creatures...). Each image carries a two-line stat caption. Ads are placed between sections.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The page is ad-dense and very long. Synergy is never explained on the page itself. The combos page lists 1,406 combos for Kess with no grouping by what they achieve, so it has the same overload problem Sim Lab has, and its usefulness drops off after the first screen.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This is the visual language Commander players read fastest: a card image with a stat caption underneath, sections named by role, and a denominator on every rate. Take: the image+caption tile for "cards that mattered in this run", the GC badge, bracket filters, and the "N card combo · +N prerequisite · results" row grammar. Avoid: the 1,406-row flat list. It is Sim Lab's 41-row table at scale.

sources_reviewed.name: Archidekt (public deck page)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The header carries exactly the facts a Commander player checks first: "Legal · Bracket: Upgraded (3) · Size: 100 · Est cost: $710.24 · Salt sum: 36.87", deck tags ("ETB Effects", "Goblins"), and author. The deck owner's own ROLE categories are the default grouping: Commander, Draw (10), Finishers (6), Haste Enabler (6), Protection, Ramp (11), Removal (8), Tokens, Tutor (3), Maybeboard. That is how players think about a list. The stats block has Colour Cost vs Production ("Cost 100% / 68 pips - 51 cards; Production 90% / 44 mana - 42 cards"), mana curve 0 to 8+, mana curve by colour, and a "Probability of draw" table. That table gives per-category odds of at least N cards by a given number drawn (Ramp 11 → 57%, Tutor 3 → 20%). A hint underneath reads "Click charts to focus on cards", so the charts act as filters on the list.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Top toolbar: Playtester, Clone, View as (Stacks / Text / Grid...), Group by (Categories / Type / MV...), Sort by, Price source, Local filter. The main area is a multi-column masonry of category stacks, each headed "Draw Qty: 10 Price: $98.00". A deck-info side panel (pinnable) holds curve, colour and probabilities. A "Condensed view" toggle and the description come after. Hovering a card name shows its image.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The toolbar is crowded with builder controls a reader doesn't need (color tags, price sources, CTRL-to-add hints leak into the reading view). Oracle text renders inline in text view, which makes the page ~17k characters long. Stats are duplicated in two places.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: the header fact line (bracket, size 100, cost), role categories as a grouping (and as the vocabulary for telemetry), charts that filter the card list, and the category odds table as the 'expected' column next to Sim Lab's 'observed' frequency. Avoid: builder chrome on a read-only analysis page.

sources_reviewed.name: Moxfield (deck page and playtester)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: It is the default deckbuilder for enfranchised Commander players, so its conventions are the baseline expectation. Text or image views, with mana cost and price optional in text view. Group by Type, Colour, CMC, Rarity or Custom Tags. Sort by name, mana cost or price. Stats include a mana curve with colour breakdown, spells vs permanents, colour ratio of cards vs mana production, average CMC, opening-hand land probability and on-curve percentage. There is a Markdown primer with a table of contents, deck history, and a playtester with hotkeys and drag-and-drop.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Moxfield's client app never got past "Loading Moxfield. This may take a minute..." in the review browser, so these notes come from Moxfield's public Features wiki plus general familiarity, not a live look. From those: a deck header with commander art and deck metadata, a view/group/sort toolbar, cards grouped in columns with counts per group, a statistics section, and tabs for Primer and Changes.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Could not be verified live this session. The notes on its general behaviour are not first-hand.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Sim Lab's deck page should meet the Moxfield baseline: a compact grouped list, hover preview (CardPreview.tsx already describes itself as "the Moxfield behaviour"), and view and group toggles. It should also count 100 cards, since Moxfield and Archidekt both count the commander. Sim Lab's analysis pages are where it can go beyond Moxfield, not the list.

sources_reviewed.name: Scryfall (card page + search in checklist mode)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Search results open with a plain-English restatement of the query: "1 – 175 of 389 cards where the card types include 'goblin' and the color identity ≤ R and it's legal in Commander." Display modes are Images / Checklist / Text Only / Full, and the mode lives in the URL (as=checklist), so every view can be shared. Checklist is a dense table (SET, №, NAME, COST, TYPE, R, ARTIST, USD, EUR, TIX). The card page has a "Faces, tokens & other parts" block linking the tokens a card makes. A TOOLBOX links out to the places players go next (EDHREC analysis, Moxfield decks, MTGTop8, Tagger). Rulings are dated. There is no decoration anywhere.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A three-column card page: the large image left, oracle text and a legality grid centre, and printings/prices, toolbox and buy links right. Rulings sit below. Search is a toolbar row (Show / as / sorted by / direction / pagination) then the results in the chosen mode.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The dense data look can feel clinical to newcomers. The site does no analysis.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: the prose restatement of the current filter (Sim Lab's prose-opener rule wants exactly this), view mode in the URL, and a Toolbox of outbound links. Scryfall's restraint is the 'crafted by people who play' feel: nothing is decorative, and every element is data or a link to more data. Oracle tags (otag:ramp, otag:removal) are a community role taxonomy Sim Lab could use for display grouping, through cached queries, never for adjudication.

sources_reviewed.name: Playgroup.gg (commander stats page + turn-order study)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: This is the best 'why' presentation found in this review. Each section is a player's question as the heading, then one computed sentence answering it, then the figures with n. "HOW DOES THIS COMMANDER WIN? When Krenko, Mob Boss wins, 62.57% of wins come via combat". It uses a fixed 7-way win-method taxonomy: Combat 62.57 / Non Combat Damage 26.18 / Combo 6.75 / Alternative 2.3 / Commander Damage 1.64 / Mill 0.45 / Poison 0.12. Other sections: "DOES SEATING ORDER MATTER?" (seat 1 47.06% n=4178 ... seat 4 23.64% n=1870). "DO MULLIGANS HURT THIS COMMANDER?". "STAPLES THAT WIN GAMES" is a win-rate lift table ranked by the 95% lower bound, with a confidence column and games count. Uncertainty is visible in the styling: "Pairs with fewer than 25 games are shown in italics; treat those as suggestive, not statistical." The turn-order page draws a dashed "fair share 25.0%" line with ±pp error bars and a "Real, or luck?" section explaining odds ratios in plain English. When logging a game, it asks for the winner "Win condition included".
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: One long single column of titled cards. Each has an uppercase eyebrow (OUTCOMES, TABLE POSITION, OPENING HANDS, HEAD TO HEAD), a question heading, a one-sentence answer, then a compact figure: a horizontal percentage bar list, a seat ladder with n under each bar, or a table. A summary paragraph sits up top ("tracked across 13,640 recorded games, winning 36% (4952–8471) at an Elo of 1,625"), followed by FAQ and related links.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Some figures are nonsensical, such as "Average damage per game 292106". There is a lot of SEO-driven FAQ padding. Tone slips into marketing on the home page.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This is the closest match to what Sim Lab is trying to say, and Commander players already read it. Sim Lab's prediction panel is fitted on "10,982 recorded human games", so adopting the same 7 win-method categories makes sim and human numbers directly comparable. Take: question headings, win-method taxonomy, n under every bar, italics for small samples, fair-share line with intervals. Avoid: FAQ padding and unsanity-checked aggregates.

sources_reviewed.name: 17lands (card data: Grades and Table views)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Every rate column sits beside its count column (# GP | GP WR, # OH | OH WR, # GIH | GIH WR, # GNS | GNS WR). The key causal-ish metric is a delta in percentage points: IIH "Improvement In Hand", e.g. Sire of Seven Deaths 10.2pp, Armasaur Guide -2.4pp. The same data has two levels of disclosure: a Grades view (A+ to F tier buckets of card names) for most readers and a Table view for experts. A "Metric definitions are here" link sits at the top. Set, format, time window and colour filters are all in the URL.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A filter bar (set, format, time period, colour pair, rarity), a Grades/Table toggle and a metric selector. Then either tier-grouped name lists or a sortable wide table with card-name hover images.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Abbreviation soup (ALSA, ATA, GIH WR, GNS) is impenetrable without the glossary. The table is wide and not mobile friendly.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: a count paired with every rate, deltas in pp for 'did this card matter', and a summary-view/expert-table toggle with a definitions link. Sim Lab's scorecards currently print every behavioural metric as prose for all four decks. A 17lands-style split (three headline figures by default, full metric table on demand) would cut the wall of numbers.

sources_reviewed.name: Grim.Cards (direct competitor: Forge-based deck gauntlet)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: It is the same premise as Sim Lab: Forge AI-vs-AI, cloud, free, coaching. Its product framing is strong: a "Deck Power Score (0–100)", an S–F grade, matchups against five named archetypes (Aggro, Control, Combo, Midrange, Ramp), and "Deck DNA" similarity. "Meet the Meta" explains why each gauntlet opponent exists in human terms: "Edgar is the speed check", "Atraxa is inevitability dressed like a board state". Its coverage diagram is plainly labelled "conceptual, not statistical". Its case study page shows good scholarly hygiene ("Correlation is not causation", minimum cohort 10 decks, CC-BY dataset).
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A marketing single-column landing page gated behind Google sign-in. The leaderboard table has columns #, DECK, FORMAT, GRADE, POWER, WIN RATE, SIMS. Explainer pages are long-form prose with stat callouts ("0–100 POWER SCORE · 5 META MATCHUPS · S–F DECK GRADE").
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Its numbers look more precise than its samples allow. The leaderboard #1 is "Angels · S · 97.3 · 93.3% · 1 sim", and five decks tie at exactly 89.7 / 86.7% from 1 sim each, which shows how coarse the score really is. The design is one challenger against a fixed field; the case study admits "a structurally expected result in a one-challenger-versus-the-field design". The copy is generic marketing ("It's the MTG deck evaluator you wish existed"), the kind of AI-slop tone the owner wants to avoid.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This is the reference to beat. Differentiate on what Grim lacks: real 4-player seat-rotated pods, archetype baselines, visible intervals and small-n styling, replays of the actual games, and a correction against human play. Borrow the 'why this opponent' explanation for the pod header. Never ship a one-decimal composite score from 8 games.

patterns.pattern: A combo is cards + prerequisites + RESULTS. 'Win' is one possible result, not a label for every combo.
patterns.seen_in: Commander Spellbook (Results: "Infinite colorless mana. Infinite storm count." for Hullbreaker + Sol Ring vs "Win the game" for Thassa's Oracle lines); EDHREC combos page (result chips, never 'win condition')
patterns.why_it_works: Enfranchised players know infinite mana does nothing without a payoff. Calling it a 'win condition' tells them the tool doesn't understand Magic, which was exactly the playtester's reaction.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: On /results/[file] (web/app/results/[file]/page.tsx around line 451), rename the "Win conditions" h2. Split each deck's combos by the `produces` list that engine/combos.py `_slim()` already stores. "Finishes the game" covers produces containing Win the game / Infinite damage / Infinite lifeloss / opponents lose. "Engine, needs a payoff" covers infinite mana, storm, ETB, untap, and names which payoff in the 99 would convert it. Show the results as small chips, as EDHREC does. Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring would then read "Engine: infinite colorless mana, infinite storm. Needs a payoff" instead of sitting next to "Converted 1".

patterns.pattern: Group variants under one combo family and highlight the swappable card.
patterns.seen_in: Commander Spellbook ("Variants grouped by combo: Yes/No"; "+ 29 variants"; "Below you find all 29 variants of this combo, with the alternative cards highlighted"). Its Hullbreaker + Selvala family swaps in Concordant Crossroads, Thousand-Year Elixir, Akroma's Memorial: the same cards as Sim Lab's Squirrel Girl rows.
patterns.why_it_works: The player's mental unit is 'Squirrel Girl plus a haste source', not 28 permutations. Grouping turns noise into a readable redundancy signal: 'you have 7 ways to give haste'.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: On the Skrat's Revenge run (sim_20260925_003803), 28 of the table's 41 rows are "The Unbeatable Squirrel Girl + {Concordant Crossroads | Thousand-Year Elixir | Akroma's Memorial | Shang-Chi | Jaheira | Elven Chorus | Citanul Hierophants | ...} + ...". Keep CSB's variant-to-combo link (`of`) in combos.py `_slim()` and render ONE row per family. For example: "Squirrel Girl + a haste source + a mana outlet · 9 haste sources and 6 outlets in the 99 · assembled 0 of 8". A disclosure lists the members. Assembled/converted become 'any member of the family'. The row count drops from 41 to about 8.

patterns.pattern: Never drop template or prerequisite pieces. Show them as a chip.
patterns.seen_in: Commander Spellbook ("+ Permanent Castable for {C}"; title "Hullbreaker Horror | Sol Ring (and one other card)"; "+2 other prerequisites", "Notable Prerequisites", "Mana Needed"); EDHREC ("+1 other prerequisite")
patterns.why_it_works: A two-card name list for a three-piece combo reads as a false claim. A row showing just the commander ("Stella Lee, Wild Card · Assembled 8 of 8 (T11)") reads as a bug.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: In the combo row, render CSB templates after the card names as a muted chip ("+ a permanent that costs {C}", "+ 1 prerequisite"). Put a Commander chip on any piece that is the deck's commander, so that "assembled 8 of 8" is plainly 'the commander was out'. Better still, don't count a line as assembled until its non-commander pieces are present. The "Stella Lee, Wild Card | Stella Lee, Wild Card | 8 of 8 (T11) | converted 2" row should never render as-is.

patterns.pattern: Answer 'how does this deck win?' with a fixed win-method taxonomy, before any combo list.
patterns.seen_in: Playgroup.gg ("HOW DOES THIS COMMANDER WIN?" Combat 62.57% / Non Combat Damage 26.18% / Combo 6.75% / Alternative 2.3% / Commander Damage 1.64% / Mill 0.45% / Poison 0.12%. It also asks "Win condition included" when a game is logged.)
patterns.why_it_works: It is the question players ask, in categories they already use at the table. It is honest about what actually ended games, and it is directly comparable with human data.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Sim Lab already has the raw material: "How games ended: 6 by combat damage, 1 by poison, 1 by draw" and each scorecard's "how it won". Promote it into a per-deck stacked bar using Playgroup's seven labels (map Forge loss lines onto them), placed ABOVE the combo section. The combo section then answers the follow-up, "Did the combos ever go off?". Because the prediction model is fitted on human games, the same labels let a later version show 'sims: 100% combat; human Krenko players: 63% combat, 26% non-combat damage'.

patterns.pattern: Section heading = the player's question. Then one computed sentence answering it. Then the figure.
patterns.seen_in: Playgroup.gg ("DOES SEATING ORDER MATTER? Krenko, Mob Boss wins 47.06% of games from position 1 and 17.82% from position 5"; "DO MULLIGANS HURT THIS COMMANDER?"; turn-order page "THE SHORT ANSWER")
patterns.why_it_works: It reads like someone who plays wrote it for someone who plays. The figure becomes evidence for a sentence instead of a puzzle, and it is the opposite of generic dashboard tiles.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Sim Lab's binding prose-opener rule already points this way, but section titles are system nouns ("What each deck did", "Win conditions", "Win-condition telemetry", "Against real playgroups"). Rewrite them as questions with a computed answer line: "How did each deck win?", "Did the combos ever go off?" ("No. Across 8 games only Kess assembled a line, once, on turn 57"), "How would this pod go against people?", and "What killed Kess?". Keep the existing notes as the fine print under each.

patterns.pattern: Every rate carries its denominator. Small samples look different.
patterns.seen_in: EDHREC ("47% inclusion · 4.04K decks / 8.66K decks"; "In 149759 decks (6.01% of 2492442)"); 17lands (# column beside every WR column); Playgroup (n= under every seat bar; "fewer than 25 games are shown in italics; treat those as suggestive, not statistical"; lift ranked "by the 95% lower bound")
patterns.why_it_works: The audience knows variance. A bare percentage from 8 games reads either as naive or as salesmanship, the way Grim's "97.3 power · 1 sim" does. A visible denominator reads as care.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The results opener already says "won 4 of 8 (50%)". Carry that into the bars. Draw a 95% interval whisker on each win-rate bar (4 of 8 is about 22–78%) next to the existing 25% fair-share marker. Set any rate with n<10 in the muted/italic style and add a legend line saying so. Replace the cryptic "From draws ~0.2" column with "expected in 8 games: 0.2". Drop the "Reading" column's repeated "draw odds predicted ~0.2; too few games to measure this" (27 identical cells) in favour of one note under the table.

patterns.pattern: Fair-share reference line plus error bars on every win-rate chart.
patterns.seen_in: Playgroup.gg turn-order page ("fair share 25.0%" dashed line; "Seat 1 · First 29.2% ±0.17pp"; "Real, or luck?" explainer)
patterns.why_it_works: In a four-player pod 25% is par. Players get the reference line instantly, and the error bar answers 'is this real?' without any statistics vocabulary.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Sim Lab already has the 25% marker ("The marker on each bar sits at 25.0%"). Add the interval whisker and a second tick for the deck's archetype baseline. SIM_CALIBRATION requires baselines beside win rates; today the baseline is not drawn on the bar. Add a one-paragraph "Real, or luck?" disclosure under the chart, written for players.

patterns.pattern: Deck header fact line: commander art, identity, bracket, 100 cards, cost, tags.
patterns.seen_in: Archidekt ("Legal · Bracket: Upgraded (3) · Size: 100 · Est cost: $710.24 · Salt sum: 36.87" + tags); EDHREC (bracket filters, GC badge); Commander Spellbook (bracket tag with reason); Moxfield (bracket and format in header)
patterns.why_it_works: Since the 2025 bracket system, bracket is the first thing a Commander player asks about any list. A header without it feels built by someone outside the hobby.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: /decks/skrat_s_revenge_239c6293.dck currently reads "The Unbeatable Squirrel Girl · 99 cards · imported". Show "100 cards", counting the commander as every deckbuilder does. Add an estimated bracket (Commander Spellbook exposes an estimate-bracket endpoint; or at least a Game Changers count) with its one-line reason. Put a small "GC" tag on Game Changer rows, and add average mana value to the fact line. On /results, show each pod deck's bracket so a mismatched pod is visible before anyone reads the win rates.

patterns.pattern: Compact grouped list with hover image by default. Full oracle text and image grid are opt-in views, kept in the URL.
patterns.seen_in: Archidekt (View as / Group by / Sort by; "Condensed view"); Moxfield (text or image view, grouping by Type/Colour/CMC/Rarity/Tags); Scryfall (Images / Checklist / Text Only / Full, as=checklist in URL); 17lands (filters in URL)
patterns.why_it_works: This audience knows the cards. Full oracle text for all 74 distinct cards in one column makes them scroll through what they already know, and the deck stops being scannable at a glance.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The Sim Lab deck page renders every card as a 46x65 Scryfall 'small' thumbnail plus full oracle text, in one column under Commander / Creatures / Artifacts and enchantments / Spells / Lands. Default to a multi-column name list with counts in the group headers ("Creatures (25)"), mana value right-aligned, and the existing CardPreview hover or focus preview. Add a view toggle: List / Visual (Scryfall 'normal' images, hotlinked) / Full text. Add a group toggle: Type / Mana value / Role. Put both in the query string (?view=visual&group=role) so a playtester can share exactly what they are looking at.

patterns.pattern: Show mana costs as symbols, never raw brace text.
patterns.seen_in: Scryfall, Moxfield, Archidekt, EDHREC and Commander Spellbook all render mana costs as symbols. None show '{1}{G}{G}{G}'.
patterns.why_it_works: Raw braces read as unfinished developer output. It is one of the strongest 'nobody polished this' signals on a Magic site.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The deck page emits `{1}{G}{G}{G}` as literal text. Sim Lab can't use WotC symbols, so either typeset costs with the commissioned pips for coloured mana plus a neutral numeral disc for generic mana, or commission a small flat 'glyph' pip set. The painted medallions at 18px (as used in the /decks colour filter) lose their detail at list size. Owner decision, but brace text should not ship.

patterns.pattern: Charts double as filters on the list beneath them.
patterns.seen_in: Archidekt ("Click charts to focus on cards": curve, colour cost vs production, category odds table)
patterns.why_it_works: The chart stops being decoration and becomes navigation: 'which of my 4-drops?' is one click. It feels hand-made because it answers the follow-up question.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Deck page: add a slim stats rail (mana curve 0 to 8+, colour pips needed vs mana produced) whose bars filter the list. Results: make the win-method bar and the "What killed it" rows clickable so they filter the Games table. For example, click "poison" and see game #1 with its Watch link, or click "Phyrexian Beast Token 72 dmg" and see the games where it hit. That links the statistics to the replays, the part only Sim Lab has.

patterns.pattern: Group by the player's own role categories, and use the same words for telemetry.
patterns.seen_in: Archidekt (owner categories: Draw 10, Ramp 11, Removal 8, Finishers 6, Haste Enabler 6, Protection 4, Tutor 3, each with draw odds); Moxfield (custom tags); Scryfall Tagger (oracle tags like otag:ramp)
patterns.why_it_works: Players already sorted their deck into roles. Telemetry that speaks that vocabulary ('you cast 1.4 ramp spells by turn 4') feels personal. Generic counters feel machine-made.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The Kess, Reanimator telemetry page leads with "No commander could be identified for this deck" (Kess is the commander) and then measures "Charge counters 0.12/g · Proliferate 0/g, Never fired". Neither has anything to do with a reanimator deck. Keep category tags when importing an Archidekt or Moxfield export, fall back to cached Scryfall oracle tags for display grouping, and build telemetry per role: ramp and draw by turn N, finishers resolved, removal cast, and for Kess, reanimation targets returned. Show Archidekt-style expected odds (hypergeometric) beside observed sim frequency.

patterns.pattern: Card image tiles with a stat caption, for 'cards that mattered'.
patterns.seen_in: EDHREC (card image grid, caption "47% inclusion / 38% synergy"); Playgroup ("STAPLES THAT WIN GAMES" lift table: "+4.6 pp · Throne of Eldraine · 206 games", ranked by 95% lower bound)
patterns.why_it_works: Players recognise cards by art faster than by name. The caption gives the one number that matters, and the format is already familiar from EDHREC.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Add a per-deck strip on /results/[file] or the telemetry tab: Scryfall images with captions like "cast in 5 of 8 · on board in 4 of 4 wins", plus a 'dealt the damage' strip using the existing "What killed it" data. Gate it: under about 20 games, title it "Showed up in wins (suggestive, 8 games)" and never rank by lift. Only on 64-game runs show a 17lands-style pp delta with the count beside it.

patterns.pattern: Link out to the tools players live in, instead of rebuilding them.
patterns.seen_in: Scryfall TOOLBOX (EDHREC, Moxfield, MTGTop8, Tagger links); Commander Spellbook ("View on EDHREC"); Playgroup (sources: Scryfall · EDHREC · JSON API)
patterns.why_it_works: It signals the tool knows its place in the ecosystem, it saves rebuilding combo steps (and rules), and it builds trust.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Link each combo family to its commanderspellbook.com/combo/{id} page (the id is already in `_slim()`), and let CSB carry the steps. The deck page gets a toolbox: "Commander on EDHREC", "Find combos on Commander Spellbook", and a link back to the original Moxfield or Archidekt URL when imported from one. Card names link to their Scryfall page. This also keeps Sim Lab clear of re-deriving card behaviour, which CLAUDE.md forbids.

patterns.pattern: Restate the current filter or query in plain English.
patterns.seen_in: Scryfall ("1 – 175 of 389 cards where the card types include 'goblin' and the color identity ≤ R and it's legal in Commander")
patterns.why_it_works: It confirms the system understood you, in your own words. This is the kind of small detail that shows a human cared.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: /decks shows the static line "43 decks. Open one to read every card." regardless of filters. Make it follow the filter ("6 of 43 decks have green in their colour identity"), and do the same on the /results index. It fits the binding prose-from-real-data rule.

patterns.pattern: Explain who is in the pod and why each opponent matters.
patterns.seen_in: Grim.Cards "Meet the Meta" ("Edgar is the speed check"; pressure axes SPEED / STACK / COMBO / SCALING / BOARD; "This coverage map is conceptual, not statistical")
patterns.why_it_works: A win rate means nothing without knowing the opposition. Naming each opponent's role makes the result readable and feels written by a player.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The results header currently reads "Kess, vs Stella vs Skrat's vs Krenko": a truncation bug at the comma in "Kess, Reanimator" that leaves a stray comma. Replace it with four commander art crops (Scryfall art_crop, as /decks already uses). Each crop gets the deck name, bracket, archetype, archetype baseline and a computed role line such as "go-wide aggro, fastest clock in the pod". The pod stops being four strings joined by 'vs'.

patterns.pattern: Two levels of disclosure: a summary view for most readers, the full metric table on demand, and a definitions link.
patterns.seen_in: 17lands (Grades view vs Table view; "Metric definitions are here"); Playgroup (one headline sentence, figures below)
patterns.why_it_works: Casual readers get the answer. Experts and investors get every metric. Neither is buried.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Each of the four scorecards prints about 12 behavioural figures ("blocked 15% of 94 attackers faced · let through 55% it could have blocked · took 91% of 11 free blocks · and 92% of the blocks it would survive · 20% of its blocks were chumps · committed 86%..."). Default each card to its headline (wins of decided games, how it won, median win round). Keep one 'notable' line that is computed, such as Stella's "86% of its blocks were chumps", and put the Blocking / Attacking / Opening hands tables behind a "Play pattern detail" disclosure with a metric glossary.

patterns.pattern: Game-list rows state winner, METHOD, round and the finishing source. No repeats, no broken values.
patterns.seen_in: Playgroup game dashboard (who dealt the most damage, knockouts, win condition recorded per game); 17lands (per-game rows with result and context)
patterns.why_it_works: The games list is the doorway to replays. Each row should say why it is worth watching.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The Games table "Decided by" column repeats the winner ("Kess, Reanimator won on round 9") and shows no method except poison. Game #6 shows "Duration NaN:NaN". "Ended T36" sits beside "round 10", two units for the same thing. Use one unit (rounds). Add a method chip (combat / poison / combo / commander damage) and the top damage source for that game, and show "–" (en dash) for missing values. Keep the Watch action as the primary.

patterns.pattern: Differentiate on honesty. Refuse a single precise-looking composite score.
patterns.seen_in: Grim.Cards leaderboard, the pitfall ("#1 Angels · S · 97.3 · 93.3% · 1 sim"; five decks tied at 89.7 / 86.7% with 1 sim each). The counter-example is Playgroup, whose note says "ELO rating alone does not tell the whole story".
patterns.why_it_works: The direct competitor sells false precision. Sim Lab's seat rotation, baselines, intervals and 'floor, not verdict' labels are a real advantage for both skeptical players and investors, if they are visible rather than buried in notes.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Don't add a 0–100 power score. Put the honesty in the primary visuals: interval whiskers, the baseline tick, italic small-n styling, a "floor" tag on combo and engine decks' win rates, and a "stdout inferred" vs "shim read" badge on replays. Say it once in the product voice: "8 games is a first look, 64 is a verdict".

research.summary:
What Commander players already expect, so Sim Lab should match it:

1. **Combo grammar.** Combos are written as "N-card combo + prerequisites leading to results", with "Win the game" as just one possible result. Variants are grouped into one combo family with the swappable card highlighted (Commander Spellbook, EDHREC).
2. **Numbers with denominators.** Every rate shows its denominator and n, and small samples are styled as suggestive (EDHREC, 17lands, Playgroup).
3. **The deck header.** Commander art, bracket, "Size: 100", cost and tags (Archidekt, Moxfield). A Game Changers badge sits next to those cards (EDHREC).
4. **The deck list.** A compact list grouped by type or by the owner's role categories, with a hover image. Full oracle text and image grids are optional views kept in the URL (Archidekt, Moxfield, Scryfall).
5. **Charts and restated filters.** Charts filter the card list (Archidekt), and the current filter is restated in plain English (Scryfall).
6. **Mana symbols, never raw braces.**
7. **Outbound links** to Scryfall, EDHREC, Commander Spellbook and the original deck URL.

The playtester's "win conditions" complaint is fully explained by that first convention. Sim Lab's table (/results/sim_20260925_003803…) has 41 rows:
- It calls every Commander Spellbook variant a win condition, including Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring. Spellbook's own Results for that combo are "Infinite colorless mana. Infinite storm count."
- It drops the template third piece ("+ Permanent Castable for {C}").
- It lists the commander alone as a combo ("Stella Lee, Wild Card · assembled 8 of 8").
- It expands one Squirrel Girl + haste-source family into 28 rows.

The data to fix this is already fetched: combos.py `_slim()` keeps `produces`. The fix is to classify by result (finisher vs engine that needs a payoff), group by Spellbook's variant-to-combo link, show template chips and a commander chip, and link each family to its Spellbook page.

**Best model for the "why".** Playgroup.gg's commander page is the best model for why-explanations. Each section is a player's question as the heading, then one computed sentence, then the figure with n. It uses a fixed seven-way win-method taxonomy (Combat, Non-combat damage, Combo, Commander damage, Poison, Mill, Alternative), a dashed fair-share line with ± error bars, and italics for samples under 25 games. Sim Lab's "How games ended" and per-deck "how it won" already hold this data. They should lead, with the combo section answering the follow-up "did the combos ever go off?". Sim Lab's prediction model is fitted on human games, so matching Playgroup's categories makes sim and human numbers comparable.

**Where Sim Lab can stand apart.** Grim.Cards is a direct competitor: Forge-based, free, with coaching and a 0–100 Power Score. Its leaderboard shows "97.3 power · 93.3% · 1 sim", with five decks tied from one sim each. Sim Lab should not copy the composite score. It should win on:
- real 4-player seat-rotated pods
- archetype baselines drawn on the bar
- visible intervals
- the "floor, not verdict" labels
- replays linked from every statistic, which no reviewed tool has

It should borrow Grim's "why this opponent" explanation for the pod header. Today that header is the truncated "Kess, vs Stella vs Skrat's vs Krenko".

**Other concrete Sim Lab defects seen while comparing:**
- The deck page renders "{1}{G}{G}{G}" as literal text, counts "99 cards" not 100, and prints full oracle text for all 74 cards in one column.
- The Kess telemetry says "No commander could be identified" and measures charge counters and proliferate, which a reanimator deck doesn't use.
- The Games table repeats the winner in "Decided by", shows "NaN:NaN" duration for the drawn game, and mixes T36 with round 10.
- The scorecards print about 12 behavioural metrics per deck as prose. The 17lands summary/table split would fix this.

**Coverage limits.** Moxfield's client app never rendered in the review browser (stuck on "Loading Moxfield"), so its notes come from its public Features wiki. TappedOut sat behind a Cloudflare challenge and was not reviewed. Screenshots were unavailable because the review tab ran in the background, so this research is text and DOM based rather than visual. No repo files were changed and no scratch notes were written.

sources_reviewed.name: Sim Lab replay theater (baseline audit, live production)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Honest board provenance: TabletopNote in Tabletop.tsx switches wording between a shim read and a stdout inference. Rounds are counted the way a table counts them, not by Forge's per-player counter. It has deep links (?t=), space and arrow keys, a Shift-arrow turn jump, one attack lane per defender, a note of which seat blocked, tokens collapsed with counts, tap and counter chips from boardfx, and an honest prose lede ('Skrat's Revenge won on round 10 via Poison from Phyrexian Beast Token').
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Two columns (.stage: 1fr plus a 330px log). Left is .theater: a status line (phase label, speed select, 'event 935 of 988'), then a 2x2 .tbl of four .parea seats (a plate with a 24px commander portrait, name, pips, a 14px life figure and a board count; a hand band; creature, noncreature and land bands). Below that come TabletopNote (3 to 4 lines of prose), then the .vcr transport (five buttons plus a scrubber with R-ticks every ceil(R/8) rounds). Under the theater sit two more notes. Right is the event log: an 81-row window centred on the playhead with 'now' and 'follows the playhead'. Measured at 1440x900: the table runs y=414 to 1179 and the transport sits at y=1256 to 1319, so play and scrub are 356px below the fold and you cannot scrub while looking at the top seats. At 375x812 the four seats stack to 1366px tall, the transport is at y=2044 and the log at y=2328.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: (1) Noise stepping: in game 1, 464 of 974 raw events are phase markers and 129 are mana events (61%), and 47 are 'didn't block X' lines. The arrow key walks through every one, and at 1x (300ms per step, uniform) a 988-step game takes about 5 minutes with an untap step dwelling as long as an elimination. (2) Tiles are 46x64px (battlefield) and 30x42px (lands and hand), using Scryfall 'small' images. Nothing is legible, and inspection goes through the native title tooltip, although useCardPreview already exists and is used by decks/[file] and playtest/[deck]. (3) BoardState.stack is computed in replay.ts but Tabletop.tsx never renders it, so spells cast and resolve invisibly. (4) The game payload carries agent_events (37 in game 1: tutor_steer 'steer=Hullbreaker Horror over=Blasphemous Act', finisher_hold 'Triumph of the Hordes creatures=1 need=3', kingmaker_reaim 'onto=Skrat's Revenge leaderThreat=10', counter_veto, block_skip) and rubric (turn 36: 15 legal blocks missed), and the replay shows none of it. (5) Event rows are not clickable: .ev has no onClick, so you cannot seek from the log. (6) Phase-label bug: the status line reads 'Round 10 · revenge's declare blockers' because replay.ts:245 matches /^(.+?)'s (.+)$/ non-greedily and splits 'Skrat's Revenge's Untap step' at the first 's. (7) Combat is text-only ('attacking Krenko →' plus red or violet borders), and the attack border uses var(--state-failed), so one colour means both 'failed' and 'attacking'. (8) Two identical 'deciding turn' links (lede and log footer). (9) Inconsistent speed labels ('1× speed', '2×', '4×'). (10) No life-over-time view, no key-moment markers, no Home/End, no '?' help. (11) The results games table mixes units ('Ended T36' next to 'won on round 10') and shows 'NaN:NaN' duration for the draw in game 6.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This is the thing being fixed. Keep the honesty machinery, round counting, per-defender lanes and deep links. Rebuild the viewport budget, stepping granularity, card legibility, the timeline and the 'why' layer.

sources_reviewed.name: 17lands game replays (MTG Arena, Limited)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Everything fits in one 1440x900 viewport, with the timeline pinned at the bottom (y≈850). Steps are coarse, so it takes 8 clicks to reach Turn 2 Main 1 with no untap or upkeep noise. The current stack item is drawn enlarged at the left under a 'Stack' label, with a yellow line to its target creature. Cards are 71x99 with state printed on them ('Tapped', 'Summoning sick', P/T '4 / 2', a purple 'A' for attacking). Every step is a URL path (/3/2/8, /3/2/40), so any moment is shareable.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Caption top-left ('Turn 4 (Player) – Main 1'). The opponent panel (life, library, graveyard and exile counts) sits over their face-down hand. Battlefield rows run in the middle, with the stack column on the far left. The player panel and hand are at the bottom. A full-width timeline follows: one segment per turn, width proportional to step count (measured widths from 6 to 122px), opponent turn numbers above and player turn numbers below, and a red playhead. Transport on the right: play, a speed select (0.5x, 1x, 2x, 4x, 8x), start, previous, next, end.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: 1v1 only. There is no text event log at all, so you have to diff board states to learn what happened. Counts use emoji icons (library, graveyard and exile), which Sim Lab's design system forbids. There is no 'why' layer and no key-moment markers. The cookie banner covers the transport on first load.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: one-viewport budget, coarse beats, stack spotlight with target line, state printed on the card, per-step URLs and proportional turn segments. Avoid: dropping the text log (Sim Lab's log is the authoritative record and must stay) and emoji glyphs.

sources_reviewed.name: HSReplay.net replay viewer (Joust)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The keyboard model is built around turns. Per the Joust user manual (github.com/HearthSim/Joust/wiki/User-manual): Space or K plays and pauses, Left and Right jump a TURN, Up and Down step an ACTION, Home and End go to start and end, W and S change speed, X reveals hidden cards, C swaps players. Keybindings are shown in scrubber tooltips, and speed persists in a cookie (CHANGELOG 0.4.0 and 0.5.0). The card just played is shown enlarged beside the board with its provenance ('Created by Schooling'). Both decklists sit beside the board and dim as cards are used. There is a 'Link to current turn' checkbox. Speeds run from 0.75x to 8x.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Left sidebar: game meta, share URL with a 'Link to current turn' checkbox, download. Centre: the board fills the height, the hero at the bottom and the opponent at the top, with the active side's half outlined. Right: both players' decklists (cost, name, count, art strip). Bottom: .joust-scrubber, a timeline split into per-turn segments ('M', 1 to 21) with alternating top and bottom classes for each player's turns and widths scaled by turn length (4 to 16px), plus a speed select and buttons. The event log is a toggle.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: At 900px viewport height the scrubber lands at y=891, barely on screen. It has no life or advantage graph and no key-moment markers. It is built for exactly 2 players (top and bottom). The mulligan screen crosses out cards with big red X images that dominate the frame.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: Left and Right move by turn, Up and Down by action; key hints in tooltips; persisted speed; the played-card spotlight with provenance; turn segments encoding whose turn it was. Adapt top and bottom to 4 lanes.

sources_reviewed.name: lichess analysis board
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Conventions every serious player already knows. Left/Right or j/k step, Up/Down (0/$) jump to start and end, f flips, and '?' opens a keyboard help overlay. The computer-evaluation graph under the board is clickable: large dots mark inaccuracies, mistakes and blunders, and each player's error list jumps to the next such move when clicked. The metric is 'winning chances', one number that swings, so the graph reads at a glance.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Board centre-left with a vertical eval bar on its edge. A move list on the right with the current move highlighted, every move clickable. Tabs below the board with the evaluation chart (current position marked by a vertical line and a dot) and per-player accuracy and error counts.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Engine numbers can feel judgemental without explanation. Beginners do not know what 'inaccuracy' means. The layout assumes 2 players and a small fixed board. (Direct navigation to lichess was blocked in the shared browser; features come from lichess forum and help pages.)
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: a clickable summary graph under the board (Sim Lab's analogue is four life lines, with seat power optional); 'jump to next key moment' from a list; a '?' overlay; every log entry a seek target.

sources_reviewed.name: chess.com Game Review
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: It separates watching from studying. 'Start Review' has a Coach at the top of the panel walk the player through key moments (last book move, brilliant move, missed tactic) in plain language, drawing arrows and highlighting squares on the board (Game Review v2). The eval graph and a report card sit at the top, and free analysis stays available. Classification icons sit on the board square of the move.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Board left with the eval bar. The right panel stacks, top to bottom: coach speech bubble, eval graph, then the move list with classification glyphs, plus a Next button that advances key moment to key moment rather than move to move.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The labels (Brilliant, Blunder) editorialise, and the site keeps redefining them after user confusion ('Game Review Common Confusion' blog). The review is gamified and pushes premium. Explanations that sound authoritative can be wrong.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: a directed 'Watch the key moments' mode separate from the stepper; a one-line plain-language caption per moment; arrows drawn on the board. Avoid: verdict labels. Sim Lab should word agent reasons as 'the AI's stated reason', not 'correct' or 'blunder'.

sources_reviewed.name: Mystmin MTGA Replay Tool
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The replay browser is a grid of game cards. Each shows both players' colour identity, the game type, a stat line ('1st | Mulls: 0 | Turns: 18 | Spells: 30 | Life: -32 +29') and a thumbnail strip of the cards each side played, so you pick the interesting game before opening it. In the viewer, identical lands collapse into a vertical stack of name strips ('Plains' x10), leaving room for battlefield cards at a readable ~130px.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Browse: a card grid with a matchup filter and a 'frequently seen' opponents list. Viewer: an Arena-style table with lands as a stacked name column on the left, permanents in a row at readable size and hands at the bottom edge.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Viewer controls are nearly invisible: only an upload button and a version select are visible, and the viewer loaded blank for about 5 seconds. There is no visible timeline or log, and there are no labels.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: game-list cards with a stat line and a final-board thumbnail for /results/[file]; lands as stacked name strips with a count so creatures get the pixels. Avoid: hidden transport.

sources_reviewed.name: mymtgo replay (MTGO log replayer)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: It states its own data ceiling: the docs say MTGO logs lack spell targets and tapped state, so replays will not show them. It offers play/pause, step, scrub and speed over snapshots of game state.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Snapshot stepper with a scrubber and speed control (the docs give no layout detail).
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Snapshot granularity with no targets. It is a generic video-player metaphor with no game-aware navigation (turns, key moments).
sources_reviewed.relevance: Confirms Sim Lab's honesty-note posture is industry-normal. Take: state the ceiling once and briefly. Avoid: a plain video-scrubber metaphor for a turn-structured game.

sources_reviewed.name: SnapComplete (Marvel Snap replay viewer)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Four arrow buttons with a clear hierarchy: the inner pair steps events within a turn (plays, reveals, triggers) and the outer pair jumps turns. Two granularities, both one click away and spatially distinct.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Turn-by-turn viewer showing locations, card placements and power totals, with nested event and turn navigation.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Marketing pages give little detail. Snap's 6-turn games need less navigation than a 36-player-turn Commander game.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: nested transport (outer = turn, inner = beat). Sim Lab already has the five buttons; the gap is that its 'step' means a raw event, not a beat.

sources_reviewed.name: SpellTable (WotC webcam Commander)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The canonical 4-player Commander information design. Each player has a horizontal bar with life total, name, commander(s) and colour identity, always visible. It offers a Focused layout (active or chosen player large, others as thumbnails in turn order) besides the 2x2 grid, a turn indicator and turn clock, and click-a-card-to-identify into a right-hand drawer with a history of identified cards.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Grid (4 equal tiles) or Focus (thumbnails in turn order on the left, one large feed on the right, an eye icon marking focus). A slim top bar per player. Card drawer on the right.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The team admits Focus-mode thumbnails can't be card-spotted (a trade-off for one-click focus switching). The 2x2 grid makes every board small.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: the player bar content order (life biggest, then name, commander, identity); a focus mode that follows the active player; turn-order thumbnails; a card drawer with history (a better home for card inspection than native tooltips).

sources_reviewed.name: Untap.in multiplayer layouts
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: It gives four layouts for 3+ players and lets users choose. Accordion keeps opponents visible across the top while the followed board expands, and you click any player to switch focus. Full Board shows only the followed player with opponents in turn order across the top. On phones a seat bar above the controls switches between opponents. The mobile card preview springs up from the bottom and drops back.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Followed board large. Opponent strips in turn order along the top. Seat bar on mobile. Bottom-sheet card preview.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Four layout modes is a lot of choice. Other opponents' details are lost while one is followed.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: Accordion as the default desktop replay layout (active seat expanded, three compact strips in turn order); the seat bar plus bottom-sheet preview for mobile, replacing today's 1366px vertical stack.

sources_reviewed.name: Cockatrice (4-player)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: A clear zone grammar: hand, then a battlefield split into lands (lower) and other permanents (upper), with the stack as its own area on the left.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Horizontal strips per player, the controlling player at the bottom. Four players become four thin horizontal bands.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The user complaint was that the 4-player UI is too cramped, with 4 lines top to bottom; the suggested fix was 4 squares. Other issues ask for resizable boards because cards become unreadable at 3+ players.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Evidence that splitting space evenly across 4 boards fails. Sim Lab's 2x2 has the same failure at 46px tiles. Give space to the seat that matters now.

sources_reviewed.name: Forge desktop match UI
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Dockable, resizable cells with tabbed panels (battlefield, hand, log, stack, card detail, combat assignments). The stack and combat each get a dedicated panel, and a large card-detail panel shows whatever is hovered.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: User-arranged cells. A big card-detail pane. Stack, combat and log as tabs.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The multiplayer defaults bunch player tabs; users drag tabs until boards sit side by side and save a layout XML (slightlymagic.net thread). Customisability stands in for good defaults.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: a persistent card-detail pane (show the hovered or spotlit card at full size rather than a tooltip); stack and combat as first-class displays. Avoid: making users arrange the layout.

sources_reviewed.name: Board Game Arena replay
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Clicking any game-log message replays from that point, and the URL gains replayfrom= so the moment is shareable. The log is the navigation.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Board centre, log on the right with each entry a seek target, replay controls in the header.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The BGA bug tracker shows 'replay from this move' sometimes jumping to the latest move, and the button is duplicated in replay mode. Two navigation systems confuse users.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: make every .ev row a button that seeks (Sim Lab's rows have no onClick today). One navigation model: log click, scrubber and keys all move the same playhead.

sources_reviewed.name: Poker hand replayers (Poker Copilot, GGPoker PokerCraft)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Street jumps (preflop, flop, turn, river) as the primary navigation. Pot, stacks and all-in equity update at each decision. Players can be anonymised for sharing. One-click 'mark important hand'. PokerCraft exports a 'Hand Moment' image and filters hands by result so the biggest swings come first.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: An oval table with seats around it and the pot in the centre. The latest action shows as a badge beside the seat that took it. A street selector plus step and autoplay.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Hands are short; the model does not scale to 36 player-turns without chaptering. Equity numbers invite over-trust.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: an action badge beside the acting seat ('Cast Triumph of the Hordes', 'Attacks with 15, 69 power'); phase jumps inside a turn (Main 1, Combat, Main 2, End) as the Commander equivalent of streets; 'biggest swing first' sorting for the game list; a shareable moment card.

sources_reviewed.name: League of Legends replay (Annotated Timeline)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The replay timeline carries icons for kills, dragons, barons, towers and inhibitors. Locking the camera on one champion brightens that champion's markers and fades the rest. The overview tab has a gold-advantage graph and where deaths happened.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A full-screen game view, a timeline strip with event icons, a per-player focus that filters marker salience, and a separate overview graph.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Icon soup when many events cluster. You have to learn the icons.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: typed key-moment markers on the scrubber (elimination, combo assembled, board wipe, big attack, commander cast), and when a seat is pinned, brighten that seat's markers. A small, consistent glyph vocabulary is needed to avoid icon soup.

sources_reviewed.name: YouTube scrubber (Most Replayed heatmap and chapters)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: A smooth intensity curve drawn directly above the progress bar shows where the action is, and you click a peak to jump. Chapters label segments on hover. Universal J/K/L keys.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Intensity sparkline fused with the scrubber. Chapter titles in the hover tooltip.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The heatmap only appears on hover on desktop. The curve has no axis, so it signals 'something happened' but not what.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: fuse a 'table intensity' curve (life lost plus permanents changed per turn, computed from logged events only) with the scrubber, and label turns on hover ('R9 · Skrat's Revenge: 15 attackers, 69 power').

sources_reviewed.name: Hearthstone Deck Tracker Twitch extension (stream overlays)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Viewers hover card names and board minions on the stream to see full card art and text, plus a stats tooltip. The decklist is draggable and can dock left or right or hide, and decks can be copied from it.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Overlay on video: a hoverable decklist rail and hover targets mapped onto board positions.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: It relies on precise hit-mapping, and hover does not exist on touch. (Commander show overlays such as Game Knights were searched, but no production documentation turned up. Their conventions of per-player nameplates with life and card pop-ups on cast are not verified here.)
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: on hover or tap, the full card plus 'where this card has been this game' (from zones). A decklist rail per seat that dims used cards (as HSReplay does) would answer 'what did this deck actually draw'.

patterns.pattern: Step by beats, jump by turns, and never make the user walk through bookkeeping
patterns.seen_in: Joust (Left/Right = turn, Up/Down = action); SnapComplete (inner arrows = events, outer = turns); 17lands (8 clicks from mulligan to Turn 2 Main 1, no untap or upkeep stops)
patterns.why_it_works: Viewers think in turns and plays, not engine ticks. Every forced stop on 'Upkeep step' is a click that teaches the user the tool is dumb.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: In lib/replay.ts, build a beats index over timeline.steps excluding kind 'phase' and 'mana' (593 of 974 raw events in game 1, 61%). Collapse consecutive "X didn't block Y" into one beat ("Kess, Reanimator didn't block 15 attackers"; 47 such lines in game 1). Arrow keys and the inner VCR buttons step beats; Shift-arrows or Up/Down and the outer buttons jump player-turns; a log toggle 'Show every engine event' keeps the full record reachable. Show the phase in the status line rather than as a step.

patterns.pattern: Board, transport and log in one viewport, with the transport pinned
patterns.seen_in: 17lands (timeline pinned at the bottom of a 900px viewport); HSReplay (board fills the height, scrubber at the bottom edge); lichess (board plus move list plus graph above the fold)
patterns.why_it_works: Scrubbing is a look-and-drag loop. If the control is off-screen from what it changes, the loop breaks and every seek costs a scroll.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Measured at 1440x900: .vcr at y=1256 to 1319, 356px below the fold; at 375x812 it is at y=2044. Make .theater height calc(100dvh minus chrome) with the board flexing and .vcr position:sticky at the bottom. Move TabletopNote out of the theater, where it sits between board and transport, into a one-line provenance chip in the status line ('Board: read from zone stream' or 'Board: inferred from log, 86% exit match') that opens the full note. Delete the duplicate page-level note 'Replays fold the event log into board state locally', which also understates shim runs.

patterns.pattern: A turn-segmented timeline that encodes whose turn it was and how much happened
patterns.seen_in: HSReplay (per-turn segments, alternating top/bottom per player, widths scaled by turn length); 17lands (segment widths 6 to 122px proportional to steps, labels above for opponent turns and below for player turns)
patterns.why_it_works: The scrubber becomes a map of the game. Long turns are visibly long, and you can aim at 'Skrat's big turn' without hunting.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Replace .scrub's R-ticks every ceil(R/8) rounds with one segment per player-turn, width proportional to beats in that turn, drawn in four thin seat lanes (seat order, marked by seat position or the commander thumbnail, never a WUBRG hue since pips are data). Round labels go on the rail and hover shows 'R9 · Skrat's Revenge · 66 events'. Clicking a segment seeks to that turn's first beat.

patterns.pattern: Typed key-moment markers with 'next key moment' navigation
patterns.seen_in: lichess (dots on the eval graph for errors; each player's error list jumps to the next one); chess.com Game Review (Next steps through key moments); LoL Annotated Timeline (kill and objective icons, brightened for the focused champion)
patterns.why_it_works: A 36-turn game has perhaps six moments that decided it. Surfacing them turns a 5-minute watch into a 30-second read, and keeps full detail one click away.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Derive markers only from logged events and the zone stream (never from oracle text, per the don't-reimplement-Magic invariant): eliminations (Seat.eliminated), the largest life swing per round (damage and life_change), mass zone changes (N or more permanents Battlefield to Graveyard in one phase = 'board wipe'), commander casts, combo pieces assembled (analysis.py's assembled turn, e.g. 'Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring assembled T57'), counterspells (agent counter_fire). Use a 4 or 5 glyph vocabulary drawn in inline SVG. Keys N and P go to the next and previous moment. Rewrite 'Jump to the deciding turn', which today is a duplicate link in the lede and the log footer, as a real list: 'Key moments (6)'.

patterns.pattern: A summary strip under the scrubber: four life lines as the Commander eval graph
patterns.seen_in: lichess evaluation chart (clickable, current position marked); LoL gold-advantage graph; YouTube Most Replayed curve fused with the progress bar
patterns.why_it_works: One glance tells you the shape of the game (who was ahead, when it swung, who got focused), and the strip doubles as a seek control.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Fold Seat.life per player-turn (the op 'life' already exists) into four small lines drawn in inline SVG above the turn segments, sharing the scrubber's x-axis. Mark each seat's line by position label and dash pattern rather than hue. A click seeks, and a vertical playhead line crosses all four. Add poison as a dotted overlay when it exists: game 1 was won by poison, and nothing in today's view would show that coming.

patterns.pattern: Show the 'why', worded as the AI's stated reason
patterns.seen_in: chess.com Coach (plain-language explanation per key moment, arrows on the board); HSReplay provenance labels ('Created by Schooling')
patterns.why_it_works: Commander players open a replay to understand why a deck won or lost. A board without reasons answers 'what', which the event log already does.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: The game payload already carries agent_events (37 in game 1) and rubric, and the replay renders neither. Attach each to the beat it annotates and show a one-line 'Why' under the status line, plus a margin glyph in the log. Examples: 'Kess searched for Hullbreaker Horror over Blasphemous Act (plan pick)'; 'Skrat's Revenge held Triumph of the Hordes: 1 creature, needs 3'; 'Stella moved her attack onto Skrat's Revenge (table leader)'; 'Kess declined 15 legal blocks' (rubric turn 36, legalMissed 15). Never label a play correct or wrong. This is also the natural home for the win-condition confusion: show when a combo piece was tutored or assembled, in context.

patterns.pattern: Spotlight the current action at readable size, with target lines
patterns.seen_in: HSReplay (the played card enlarged beside the board); 17lands (the stack item enlarged in a 'Stack' column, a yellow line to its target); Forge (a dedicated stack panel and a big card-detail pane)
patterns.why_it_works: The eye needs one place to look each beat. Otherwise a 25-permanent board changes silently, and at 46px nobody can tell what changed.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Render BoardState.stack (computed in replay.ts, never drawn in Tabletop.tsx) as a centre spotlight: the top stack object as a hotlinked Scryfall 'normal' image (~220px wide) with 'Cast by Skrat's Revenge' and, where the log names one, the target, plus a thin connector to the target's tile or seat. Fade it on stack_resolve. 66 stack_add and 63 stack_resolve beats in game 1 are currently invisible except as log text.

patterns.pattern: Combat drawn as arrows between seats, with totals
patterns.seen_in: MTG Arena and 17lands target lines; poker action badges beside the acting seat
patterns.why_it_works: In multiplayer the question is who swung at whom, and with how much. Red borders on 30 tiles scattered across two quadrants do not answer it.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: An SVG layer over .tbl draws one arrow per Lane (already one per defender) from the attacking seat's centre edge to the defender's, labelled 'Skrat's Revenge: 10 attackers, 50 power → Krenko'. Blocks are short connectors on the defender's side. Totals come from rubric (attackPower, incomingPower, lifeTaken) or from summed zone pt. Give attack its own token instead of reusing --state-failed: today one colour means both 'failed' and 'attacking', which breaks DESIGN_SYSTEM's one-meaning-per-colour rule.

patterns.pattern: Follow the active seat and compact the others
patterns.seen_in: SpellTable Focused layout (large active feed, thumbnails in turn order); Untap.in Accordion and Full Board (followed board expands, opponents in turn order across the top; seat bar on phones); Cockatrice users on the cramped even split
patterns.why_it_works: Only one seat is acting at a time. An even 2x2 gives every board a quarter of the space and makes all four unreadable.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Default desktop layout: the active seat's .parea expands to roughly 60% of the stage, and the other three become compact strips in turn order (portrait, life, hand count, board count, top threats by power, face-down count for the rest). It auto-follows during play; clicking a strip pins it and shows a 'Following: Kess (pinned)' chip. On mobile, a seat bar of four tabs, each with life, sits above a single board; swipe switches seats and the log becomes a bottom sheet.

patterns.pattern: Cards legible at a glance, fully inspectable on demand
patterns.seen_in: 17lands (71x99 tiles with 'Tapped', P/T and attack state printed on the card); Mystmin and Arena (lands as stacked name strips with counts); Joust (full card on hover); Untap.in (mobile preview springs up from the bottom); Forge (card-detail pane)
patterns.why_it_works: An enfranchised player recognises a card by art and name in under a second, but not at 46x64. Native title tooltips are slow, unstyled and absent on touch.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Swap the title-attribute tooltip in Tabletop.tsx Tile for the existing useCardPreview (already used by decks/[file] and playtest/[deck]), with a tap-to-open bottom sheet on touch. Render lands as stacked name strips with a count ('Forest ×7'), which frees about 40% of each seat's height for creatures at 72px or wider (Scryfall 'normal' or 'art_crop' plus a name bar). Keep P/T and counters as always-visible chips. Hover should also show 'this game: drawn R3, cast R5, died R8' from zones.

patterns.pattern: The log is a navigation surface
patterns.seen_in: Board Game Arena (click any log message to replay from there, with replayfrom= in the URL); lichess move list (every move clickable)
patterns.why_it_works: Users read the log to find a moment, then want to see it. Making them transcribe the moment into scrubber position is friction.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Make each .ev row a button (onClick seek(i), Enter and Space, visible focus ring). Group rows under sticky turn headers ('Round 10 · Skrat's Revenge', collapsible), and add filter chips (Casts, Combat, Life, Zone changes, Why). Replace the 81-row window with a virtualised full list so 'find the turn Kess tutored' works by scrolling or Ctrl-F.

patterns.pattern: Discoverable keyboard and persisted playback preferences
patterns.seen_in: lichess ('?' opens the shortcut overlay); Joust (keybindings shown in scrubber tooltips, speed saved in a cookie, W/S speed); YouTube (J/K/L)
patterns.why_it_works: Power users live on the keyboard, but only if they can find the keys. Resetting the speed on every game punishes people who watch several games.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Add Home and End, N and P for key moments, 1 to 4 to pin a seat, and '?' to open an overlay listing every key. Put hints into button titles ('Next turn (Shift →)'). Widen speeds to 0.5x, 1x, 2x, 4x and 8x with consistent labels (today '1× speed', '2×', '4×'), and persist speed in localStorage wrapped in try/catch, a per-viewer convenience the artifact and design rules allow. Retire the separate 'Keyboard:' paragraph under the theater.

patterns.pattern: Two ways to watch: a directed 'Watch' mode and a free 'Study' mode, with pacing by importance
patterns.seen_in: chess.com ('Start Review' walks the key moments, free analysis always available); broadcast replays (dwell on big plays, skip bookkeeping)
patterns.why_it_works: Most visits are lean-back ('show me how Skrat won'), some are lean-forward ('what did Kess hold on turn 23'). One uniform 300ms tick serves neither.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Watch (default play button): plays beats with dwell by type (about 0.6s for land and mana, 1.2s for cast and resolve, 1.8s for combat damage, 3s with a caption for key moments and eliminations) and auto-follows the active seat. Study is the stepper. Today 1x equals 300ms times 988 steps, about 5 minutes, with untap steps given the same weight as eliminations.

patterns.pattern: Pick the game before you open it: game lists as story cards
patterns.seen_in: Mystmin browse (game cards with colour identity, 'Mulls / Turns / Spells / Life' stat line and a thumbnail strip of played cards); PokerCraft (filter by result, biggest hands first); 17lands (replay linked from event history)
patterns.why_it_works: In an 8 or 16 game run the user wants the combo turn or the blowout, not game #4. A table of identical 'Watch' links hides that.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: On /results/[file], replace the Game/Winner/Ended/Duration/Decided by/Replay table. Today it mixes 'Ended T36' (Forge player-turns) with 'won on round 10', shows 'NaN:NaN' for the game-6 draw, and repeats 'Draw (draw)'. Use one card per game: rounds only, how it ended, a one-line story from key moments ('Skrat swung 69 power across two opponents in round 9'), mulligans per seat, and a strip of the deciding cards (hotlinked Scryfall art). Offer sorts by 'biggest swing' and 'combo assembled'.

patterns.pattern: Seat identity by portrait and position, with life as the loudest number
patterns.seen_in: SpellTable player bar (life, name, commander, colour identity, always visible); 17lands player panel (life plus library, graveyard and exile counts)
patterns.why_it_works: Life is the most-glanced number at a Commander table, and graveyard size matters to half the archetypes (Kess is a reanimator deck).
patterns.apply_to_simlab: In .plate, enlarge the commander portrait from 24px to about 40px and life from 14px to about 22px mono, with a brief delta flash (+3 or -14) on change; motion only on change, never a glow, since glow is reserved for the primary and live activity. Add library, graveyard and exile counts from the zone stream on shim runs, drawn as inline-SVG glyphs (never emoji), plus poison and commander-damage chips when non-zero. Fix the status line's 'revenge's declare blockers': replay.ts:245's non-greedy /^(.+?)'s (.+)$/ splits deck names with apostrophes, so match against the known player keys instead.

patterns.pattern: Stable, shareable moments
patterns.seen_in: 17lands (each step is a path segment, /3/2/40); HSReplay ('Link to current turn' checkbox); Joust (startAtTurn); BGA (replayfrom=)
patterns.why_it_works: Playtesters report problems by sending a moment, and a link that drifts after a code change destroys the evidence.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: ?t= is an index into timeline.steps, so any change to folding (like the beats index above) silently repoints old links. Encode Forge's stable event seq and the round, as in ?r=10&seq=931, and offer both 'Copy link to this moment' and 'Copy link to this turn' as an icon button beside the scrubber, not a header button labelled 'Copy link at this event'.

research.summary:
Across every replay viewer that works (17lands, HSReplay/Joust, lichess, chess.com Game Review, SnapComplete, BGA, poker replayers, LoL), the same contract holds. The board, the transport and a record of what happened fit in one viewport. Navigation moves in the units people think in (turns and plays, not engine ticks). The timeline is a map of the game (per-turn segments, key-moment markers, a summary curve like the lichess eval graph). The thing that just happened is shown big (HSReplay's played-card spotlight, 17lands' stack card with a target line). The best viewers add a layer explaining why (chess.com Coach). None of the Magic-specific tools handles 4 players well: Cockatrice users call the 4-player board cramped; Forge users drag tabs by hand; SpellTable and Untap.in solve it by focusing the active or chosen seat and compacting the rest in turn order, plus a seat bar on phones. MTG Arena and MTGO have no native replays, and Legends of Runeterra trackers (Mobalytics) are sunset, so this is open ground.

Sim Lab's replay has better honesty machinery than any of them, but it breaks the contract in measurable ways:
- At 1440x900 the play and scrub controls sit 356px below the fold (y=1256), and at 375x812 they sit at y=2044, under a 1366px stack of four seats.
- 61% of the steps you arrow through are phase or mana bookkeeping (593 of 974 raw events in game 1), plus 47 separate "didn't block" lines. At 1x, a uniform 300ms tick takes about 5 minutes to play one game.
- Cards are 46x64 and 30x42px Scryfall "small" images, inspectable only through native title tooltips, although useCardPreview already exists elsewhere in the app.
- The stack is computed (BoardState.stack) but never drawn.
- The payload already carries the agent's stated reasons (agent_events: "steer=Hullbreaker Horror over=Blasphemous Act", "Triumph of the Hordes creatures=1 need=3", kingmaker re-aims) and a block rubric (15 legal blocks declined on the final turn), and none of it is shown. That layer is what would make this replay unlike anything else in Magic.
- Log rows are not clickable.
- The status line reads "revenge's declare blockers" because of a non-greedy regex at replay.ts:245.
- Attack borders reuse the "failed" status token.
- The games table mixes Forge turns with table rounds and shows "NaN:NaN" for a draw.

The recommended shape:
1. One-viewport theater with a sticky transport.
2. Accordion layout that follows the active seat, with three compact strips in turn order; seat-bar tabs plus a bottom-sheet log on mobile.
3. Beat-level stepping, turn jumps and key-moment jumps (N/P), plus a "?" overlay and persisted speed.
4. A timeline of per-turn segments in four seat lanes, with typed key-moment glyphs and four life lines, all derived from logged events and the zone stream, never from oracle text.
5. A centre spotlight for the stack and SVG combat arrows between seats, with totals.
6. A clickable, turn-grouped, filterable log with "Why" notes worded as the AI's stated reason, never as a verdict.
7. A default "Watch key moments" mode paced by importance, beside a free "Study" stepper.
8. Game-list story cards so users open the interesting game first.

All of this fits the binding constraints: Scryfall images stay hotlinked; the shim or inferred provenance note stays but shrinks to a status-line chip that opens the full text; seats are told apart by portrait, position and dash pattern, never WUBRG hue; glow stays on play and live activity only; no emoji. Evidence limits: lichess could not be browsed directly (its features come from lichess forum and help pages); SnapComplete and poker-replayer details come from vendor pages; Commander show overlays (Game Knights and similar) could not be verified from production sources, so no claims are made about them.

sources_reviewed.name: Sim Lab home page (live)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The honesty note under Top decklists ('Pooled across every pod and seat... Built from 25 of 46 runs') is careful, human and specific. Recent sims have one link per row and no repeated 'Watch' column. The footer legal lines are present and readable.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: This is the standard AI landing page, top to bottom. A centred 200px mascot sits over a centred Cinzel wordmark on purple and cyan storm art. Below that is a 4-tile stat strip ('43 decks on this engine / 317 games simulated / 46 finished runs / 3,152 rules loaded'), each tile decorated with a W, U, R or C pip. Then the centred prompt 'What would you like to do today?' over four equal uppercase CTA tiles (RUN NEW SIMULATION with cyan glow, SIM HISTORY & ANALYTICS in violet, IMPORT DECK, EXPLORE DECKS) that repeat the top nav one for one. A tiny mono line follows ('two decks ≈ 5 s a game · four decks ≈ 8 min for 16'), then a single glass panel holding two lists.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: (1) Run titles are machine-truncated: 'Kess, vs Power vs Talrand vs Kambal', 'Kess, vs Skrat's vs Stella vs Krenko'. shortName() in web/lib/format.ts keeps everything before the first space, so the comma stays. (2) Top decklists is sorted by most run and draws win-rate bars (8%, 13%, 59%) that its own footnote says not to compare.
