(3) The cost hint says 8 min for four decks over 16 games; CLAUDE.md's measured typical run is 40 to 105 min. (4) '4 games' runs get a winner at '25%'. (5) Every tab is titled 'Arcane Sim Lab'. (6) Nothing shows a returning user their own latest run, their decks or a running job.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Take: the honest footnote voice. Avoid: the whole hero, stat strip, prompt and four-CTA structure. It is the most recognisable AI-slop composition there is, and DESIGN_SYSTEM.md §5 and §6 specify it literally, including the copy line.

sources_reviewed.name: Sim Lab results page, the playtester's run (live)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: It opens with a real computed sentence. Seat rotation and the 25% even-share marker are stated. The four deck scorecards are small multiples at the same scale. The 'Against real playgroups' block states its error ('±4.0 points typical error', 'rank correlation 0.48') and tells the reader to read the ranking before the point estimate, which is excellent. 'How games ended' is a plain-language finding.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Title and meta, the primary 'WATCH A WINNING GAME' top right, a prose opener, then a 4-figure strip (8 games / 12 median rounds / 50% / 1 draw) that repeats the sentence right above it. Next come four scorecards with about 14 generated micro-sentences each ('held a blocker that survives the table's biggest attacker 15% of the time'), the prediction table, How games ended, a Win conditions table of 38 rows (28 of them Skrat's Revenge variants), and a games table with a text filter for 8 rows.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: (1) Win conditions lists Commander Spellbook variants as wins: 'Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring' (Spellbook itself says it produces infinite colourless mana and storm, not a win), 'Stella Lee, Wild Card' (just the commander, '8 of 8 assembled'), and 28 near-identical Squirrel Girl rows each reading 'draw odds predicted ~0.2; too few games to measure this'. (2) At 1280px the table scrolls sideways and clips the most useful column, 'Piece most often missing'. (3) The prediction table centres its headers over left-aligned numbers, and corrections use a hyphen, not a true minus. (4) Game #6 shows 'NaN:NaN' duration and 'Draw (draw)'. (5) Time units are mixed: 'T36' next to 'won on round 10', and 'Assembled 1 of 8 (T57)'. (6) The same deck shows two denominators: '4 of 7 57%' in its card, 50.0% in the prediction table. (7) Kess wins carry the filled square that means 'done' in the status system, and the draw carries the hollow 'queued' circle, so one shape means two things.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Keep the prose opener, the prediction block's calibrated voice and the small multiples. Rebuild win conditions around what a combo produces, collapse its variants, and fix table alignment and units.

sources_reviewed.name: Sim Lab replay, game 1 of the same run (live)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Keyboard transport (space; arrows; shift+arrows by turn) is documented on the page. There is a 'Jump to the deciding turn' link, 'Copy link at this event' deep links, round ticks on the scrubber, and identical tokens stacked with a count ('10'). Bottom seats are mirrored like a real table. The honesty note distinguishes the zone stream from inference.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Inside the 1280px page: a 4-quadrant tabletop (measured 828px wide, 917px tall), a transport bar under it, and a 330px event log to the right. Each quadrant holds a name plate, then Hand, Lands and an 'Artifacts, enchantments and unidentified' row. Measured card sizes at a 1440px viewport: 28x40px for hand and lands, 44x62px for permanents, 29x20px for tapped lands.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: (1) Cards are too small to recognise. The board uses about 57% of a 1440px screen while the backdrop fills the rest. On a 1440x900 laptop the transport controls sit below the fold. (2) The log is raw Forge output. Every step of every player's turn appears (Untap, Upkeep, Draw ... Cleanup) even when nothing happens. Mana abilities appear as events ('Forest - {T}: Add {G}.'). Reminder text appears as its own event ('Flashback {1}{G} (You may cast...)'). Engine debug text leaks ('[Card: Chatter of the Squirrel, Activator: Skrat's Revenge, SpellAbility: ...]'), along with instance ids ('Phyrexian Beast Token (995)'), missing spaces ('Krenko Goblins(as poison counters)'), a 17-attacker declaration in one line and 12 'didn't block' lines in a row. (3) Seat plates read 'Kess,' and the phase label reads 'revenge's untap'. (4) Krenko shows '46 poison' and Stella '19 poison' while still drawn as live seats. (5) There is no life-over-time view and no key-moment list.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This screen needs the most care, because watching a replay is the emotional core of a card-game simulator. Rebuild it as a broadcast view: a legible board that fits the viewport, a life chart as the scrubber, key moments, and the log on demand.

sources_reviewed.name: Sim Lab DESIGN_SYSTEM.md (binding Arcane spec) and mockups/design_principles.md (the superseded research)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: The accessibility contract is real: measured contrast ratios, status shown by shape, a 2px focus ring, reduced motion honoured. The em-dash rule forces sentences to say what they mean. 'Fixes subtract' (law 5) is a genuinely good law. The IP-safe painted pips are a distinctive, owned asset.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: It prescribes the home order verbatim: 'header + mascot → rolling tally banner → "What would you like to do today?" + action hub → two-column data panel'. It also prescribes four equal-footprint uppercase action buttons, glass on art on every screen, Space Grotesk body and JetBrains Mono data, and ships the Midjourney prompt used for the backdrop ('--ar 16:9 --v 6.0').
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: design_principles.md Part 1, the repo's own earlier research, lists as AI tells: glassmorphism and aurora glows (#2), stat-card banners (#3), all-caps labels (#6), Space Grotesk combos (#8) and the centred hero (#9). The Arcane reskin adopted five of them on purpose. Its structural rules still bind (prose opener, one primary, honesty notes), but the visual spec now encodes the slop the earlier research warned about. The 'never disable the primary' rule is applied mechanically: the coaching page shows a glowing 'GENERATE COACHING REPORT (~$0.01, ABOUT 20 S)' next to copy saying 'the button above will fail. Set MTG_LLM_API_KEY in deploy/.env and redeploy', which is operator instructions shown to end users.
sources_reviewed.relevance: The owner may change the spec, and there is a strong case to: remove §5's home order, the §6 tally banner and action hub, and glass behind data; replace the Space Grotesk body face; keep the a11y contract, the status shapes, the pips, the em-dash rule and law 5.

sources_reviewed.name: Nielsen Norman Group: 10 Usability Heuristics
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Technology-agnostic criteria that turn 'feels janky' into diagnosable defects.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Ten heuristics. The ones that bite Sim Lab: #2 match between system and real world (speak the user's language, not internal jargon), #4 consistency and standards, #6 recognition rather than recall, #7 flexibility and efficiency (accelerators for experts), #8 aesthetic and minimalist design (no irrelevant information), #9 plain-language errors.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Heuristics catch defects, not character. A page can pass all ten and still look generic.
sources_reviewed.relevance: #2 is violated wherever engine vocabulary reaches the screen ('T36', '(995)', '{T}: Add {G}', raw filenames, 'Draw (draw)'). #8 is violated by the stat strip that repeats the opener and by 28 variant rows. #9 is violated by the coaching page's deploy instructions.

sources_reviewed.name: NN/g: 8 Design Guidelines for Complex Applications
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Written for expert domain users who want power, not simplification.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: The relevant guidelines: #6 reduce clutter without reducing capability (staged disclosure), #7 ease the move between primary and secondary information without leaving the screen, #8 make important information visually salient by removing what competes with it.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: 'Expert' does not mean 'show everything at equal weight'. Salience still has to be designed.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Commander players are experts. Keep blocking and attacking telemetry and the raw log, but stage them. The replay's default view should be key moments, with the full log a toggle away (#6, #7). The deciding swing should be the most salient thing on the replay (#8).

sources_reviewed.name: Developers Digest: 16 AI design slop patterns
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: A concrete, checkable list of tells rather than vague taste.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Fonts: Inter everywhere, repeated Space Grotesk/Instrument Serif/Geist combos. Colour: lavender-purple, permanent dark mode with grey text and all-caps labels, gradients, coloured glows. Layout: centred hero, badge above H1, coloured card borders, identical feature cards, numbered steps, stat banner rows, emoji sidebar, all-caps headings.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Some items are fashion rather than usability. The fix is intent, not a blanket ban on dark mode.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Sim Lab's home hits #2, #5, #7, #8, #9, #12, #14 and #16. The fix it suggests for stat banners, putting the stats into the narrative, is exactly Sim Lab's own prose-opener rule.

sources_reviewed.name: SmoothUI and Superdesign on AI design slop (2026)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Explains why slop happens: models reach for the statistical median. It names the purple-to-cyan gradient plus glassmorphism plus neon glow plus identical card grid as the default, and notes that polished slop is harder to spot.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Signs: purple-cyan gradients, glass with neon glow, identical card grids, bounce hovers, undesigned empty and error states. Fix loop: build with guardrails, critique against explicit criteria, fix the highest-impact issue, repeat.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Vendor posts pitch their own tooling.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Sim Lab's palette is literally cyan (#00E5FF) and violet (#A855F7) with glow over purple storm art. 'Undesigned states' matches NaN:NaN, the empty command zone in playtest, and a coaching primary that always fails. https://superdesign.dev/blog/why-ai-design-looks-generic

sources_reviewed.name: Anthropic frontend-design skill / 'frontend aesthetics' prompt
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: States the model-side cause precisely. Its wording: 'NEVER converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations', and avoid 'predictable layouts and component patterns, and cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character'.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Commit to one aesthetic direction drawn from the context, then execute it with precision. Restrained designs need precise spacing and typography, not effects.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Aimed at generators, so it pushes novelty. Sim Lab needs fit to domain more than novelty.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Space Grotesk is Sim Lab's body face and is named as the font models converge on. It is a literal fingerprint of Claude-built UI. Replace it with a face chosen for a reason, such as legibility of dense card names and tabular figures.

sources_reviewed.name: 'Usable but Conventional' (arXiv 2605.15124, n=92, UEQ-S)
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Empirical: blind participants rated AI-generated prototypes positively on pragmatic qualities and neutral to negative on originality and novelty.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: n/a (study)
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Prototype-level study, not long-term use.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This backs the owner's instinct. Sim Lab can be usable and still read as generated. The fix is domain character, not more polish.

sources_reviewed.name: Apple HIG: Materials / Liquid Glass
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Even the company that shipped glass as a system says: 'Don't use Liquid Glass in the content layer'. Glass belongs to the control and navigation layer; lists, tables, media and scrolling content get standard materials, and glass should never stack.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Two layers. Content (documents, lists, tables) sits on solid material. Functional chrome (bars, controls, transient overlays) floats on glass.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Liquid Glass itself drew wide legibility criticism, which is the point.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Sim Lab puts every table, scorecard and event log on 0.85 glass over busy art. Invert that: data on opaque ground, with glass reserved for the top bar and the replay transport.

sources_reviewed.name: Material Design density guidance
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Treats density as a deliberate scale. Dense components suit data-rich scanning and comparison; as components get denser, margins and gutters grow; horizontal padding goes up as vertical spacing comes down.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A density scale of 0 to -3 in 4px steps, with tables and long lists as the prime candidates.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Controls that change settings keep full-size targets.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Scorecards and tables can go denser (about 32 to 36px rows, right-aligned figures). Put the saved space into the replay board, which needs size, not the tables.

sources_reviewed.name: Tufte: data-ink, chartjunk, small multiples, sparklines
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: 'Above all else, show the data'. Erase non-data ink and redundant data ink. Use small multiples of the same chart at the same scale, and word-sized sparklines inside text. Keep graphical integrity: every number needs its comparison.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Small repeated panels on shared axes, and inline sparklines.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Pure minimalism can strip affordances. Keep hover and click cues.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Remove the redundant ink (the stat strip, pips as ornament in the banner, 28 variant rows). Add the missing data: a per-seat life sparkline in each scorecard and on each games-table row, plus a 4-line life chart as the replay scrubber.

sources_reviewed.name: Dieter Rams: ten principles ('less but better')
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Good design is honest (it does not pretend to be what it is not), understandable, unobtrusive, thorough down to the last detail, and 'as little design as possible'.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: n/a (principles)
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Easy to cite and hard to apply. It needs concrete checks.
sources_reviewed.relevance: 'Honest' applies to telemetry claiming 'Charge counters 0.12/g · Partial' for a reanimator deck, and to a primary button that will fail. 'Thorough down to the last detail' applies to NaN:NaN, 'Kess,' and clipped columns, which are exactly what makes something read as unattended. 'Unobtrusive' applies to the backdrop behind data.

sources_reviewed.name: MTG Arena phase ladder redesign
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Arena made the phase ladder deliberately minimal because it 'often distracted from more important information'. The ladder is a quick-glance element. The combat sub-steps expand only during combat (the damage icon splits when first strike applies), and a turn marker shows whose turn it is.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: A compact horizontal ladder of phase glyphs with the current phase lit, and a combat mini-ladder that appears only in combat.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: It is a play client's control. Sim Lab must present it as read-only indication, never as stops.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Replace the dozens of 'X's Upkeep step' log lines with a read-only phase ribbon on the replay stage. Log lines then only appear when something happened.

sources_reviewed.name: Commander Spellbook combo results
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: Every combo is stated as cards plus what they produce. Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring is listed with results 'Infinite colorless mana' and 'Infinite storm count', and variants are grouped under 'see all possible replacements'.
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Cards, then results, prerequisites, steps and an EDHREC popularity count, with variants folded behind one combo.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: The raw variant list is exhaustive by design. Spellbook is a search index, not an analysis.
sources_reviewed.relevance: Sim Lab removed the results field and relabelled every variant a 'win condition'. The domain-native fix is to show 'Produces: infinite colourless mana, infinite storm', group rows into 'wins by itself', 'engine (needs a payoff in the deck: X, Y)' and 'not a combo', and fold variants under their shared core.

sources_reviewed.name: lichess / chess.com game review
sources_reviewed.what_it_does_well: A replay made for learning: an advantage graph across the whole game where sharp swings mark the decisive moves, and clicking a swing or a flagged blunder jumps there. A coach line sits at the top and guides the viewer through key moments. The move list is the secondary view. https://lichess.org/forum/game-analysis/lichess-analysis-and-some-beginner-doubts-about-it
sources_reviewed.layout_pattern: Board centre stage and large. The eval graph doubles as the timeline. Key moments are a short clickable list. The full move list and engine lines are toggles.
sources_reviewed.pitfalls: Chess.com's redesign hid the graph during review and drew complaints. Do not hide the overview behind the step-through.
sources_reviewed.relevance: This is the right model for 'how people want to watch a replay': overview first (who was ahead when, and what swung it), then jump to moments, then step through actions. It stays viewing-only, so it does not cross the gameplay-client line.

patterns.pattern: REMOVE (slop): the hero + stat strip + chatbot prompt + four-CTA hub home composition
patterns.seen_in: Sim Lab home (mascot over wordmark, '43 decks on this engine' strip, 'What would you like to do today?', four equal uppercase tiles repeating the nav). Developers Digest #9, #12, #14, #16. design_principles.md Part 1 #3 and #9.
patterns.why_it_works: Removing it works because this exact composition is the modal output of generators, so experts read it as unattended in about a second. The stat strip holds vanity numbers ('3,152 rules loaded') no Commander player cares about. The four tiles duplicate the top nav, so the page spends its best real estate on navigation that already exists.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Replace DESIGN_SYSTEM.md §5's home order and §6's tally banner and action hub. Keep a compact masthead: wordmark plus a mascot head of 48px at most, left-aligned or small. Beneath it, what a returning player wants, in order: (a) a running job with live progress, or your latest run as one sentence ('Kess won 4 of 8 against Stella Lee, Squirrel Girl and Krenko, all by combat. Watch the deciding game.') with four commander art crops; (b) one primary 'Simulate a pod' with the honest duration ('about 40 to 105 min for four decks over 16 games'); (c) your decks as commander art tiles. Drop the stat strip entirely. If the rules count matters, it belongs on /rules.

patterns.pattern: REMOVE (slop): glass-and-glow over AI art behind content; keep art to one ceremonial place
patterns.seen_in: Every Sim Lab page puts tables and the event log on 0.85 glass over purple and cyan storm art (the DESIGN_SYSTEM ships its Midjourney prompt). The telemetry page's glass panel is half empty. Apple HIG: don't use glass in the content layer. SmoothUI: purple-to-cyan plus glass plus neon glow is the slop default.
patterns.why_it_works: Reading data on moving, high-contrast art costs attention on every glance (Rams: unobtrusive; Tufte: non-data ink). The palette of cyan #00E5FF and violet #A855F7 with glow is the single most recognised 'AI app' look of 2025 and 2026.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Results, telemetry, coaching, replay, decks and rules get an opaque near-black ground (a solid --bg-void or a subtle paper-like surface), with no backdrop and no blur. The backdrop stays only behind the home masthead and on empty or 404 states. Glow survives only on a live running job, as the spec already says; stop glowing the always-visible primaries. Redefine the art as 'a stage for ceremony, never behind reading' in DESIGN_SYSTEM §11.

patterns.pattern: REMOVE (slop): converged typography (Space Grotesk body, mono everywhere, uppercase CTAs)
patterns.seen_in: globals.css body font 'Space Grotesk'. JetBrains Mono slashed zeros in every table ('0 of 8'). Uppercase two-line CTA labels ('RUN NEW SIMULATION', 'GENERATE COACHING REPORT (~$0.01, ABOUT 20 S)'). Anthropic frontend-design skill names Space Grotesk; Developers Digest #2 and #16.
patterns.why_it_works: Type is the first thing a trained eye fingerprints. A body face chosen because generators choose it reads as generated. Mono for every figure gives tables a terminal look and wastes width; slashed zeros add visual noise to columns that are mostly zeros.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Pick a body face for a stated reason: dense card names at 13 to 14px plus good tabular figures. Candidates to evaluate: Source Sans 3, IBM Plex Sans or Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (a legibility story that fits the a11y contract). Set tabular-nums in that face for table figures and reserve mono for run ids, filenames and seeds. Buttons in sentence case at 14 to 15px ('Simulate a pod', 'Watch the deciding game'). Keep Cinzel once, for the wordmark.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: the commander is the atom of identity (art crop + short commander name + pips), never a string-truncated deck name
patterns.seen_in: Moxfield, Archidekt and EDHREC all lead with commander art. Sim Lab's own /new deck picker does this well (art crop, name, pips). Failures: shortName() in web/lib/format.ts produces 'Kess, vs Stella vs Skrat's vs Krenko' (home, results title, replay plates 'Kess,'), and the replay phase label reads 'revenge's untap'.
patterns.why_it_works: Commander players recognise a deck by its commander's face faster than by any text (recognition over recall, NN/g #6). Dangling commas and possessive fragments are the kind of tiny carelessness that makes something read as machine-made.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Derive a display name from the commander: the part before the comma of the commander's card name ('Kess', 'Stella Lee', 'Krenko'), or the full deck name when two collide, and never a first whitespace token. Put a 24 to 32px circular art crop (Scryfall art_crop, hotlinked) beside every deck mention: run titles, scorecard headers, replay seat plates, games-table winner cells, recent sims. Titles become 'Kess vs Stella Lee vs Squirrel Girl vs Krenko'. Where the commander is unknown ('No commander could be identified' for Kess Reanimator), fix the data rather than showing an empty command zone in playtest.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: replay as a broadcast/analysis view: overview chart, key moments, legible board, log on demand
patterns.seen_in: lichess advantage chart (click a swing to jump), chess.com Game Review key moments with a coach line, MTG Arena's minimal phase ladder. Sim Lab replay today: 28x40px and 44x62px cards; a 917px-tall theater that pushes transport below the fold at 1440x900; a 330px raw log dominated by step lines.
patterns.why_it_works: People watch a replay to answer 'what swung it and could I have survived it'. An overview-first view answers that in five seconds; stepping through 980 events does not. Legible cards are the minimum bar for Magic: an expert identifies a card by its art at about 90px or wider, and not at 44px.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Stage layout that fits in 100vh: drop the 1280px max-width for a 'theater' mode. Board takes about 70% of width. Battlefield creatures render as art-crop tiles about 96px wide with a P/T badge and a tapped rotation. Lands collapse to a mana row ('7 lands: 3 Forest, 2 Island, …' with a count). Tokens stack with ×N. Eliminated seats grey out with 'Out on turn 9 (poison)'. Across the top, a 4-line life chart (one line per seat, commander-art legend, x = turn) is the scrubber: click to seek, with diamonds for key moments (commander cast, wrath, combo assembled, elimination, lethal swing). A key-moments list sits beside the board. A read-only phase ribbon replaces step lines. The transport is sticky. The raw event log becomes a toggle tab, filtered by default to actions (cast, attack, block, damage, dies, exiled, life change), with runs collapsed ('didn't block 12 attackers'). Strip mana abilities, reminder text, '[Card: … SpellAbility: …]' and instance ids unless the same name repeats. This is all viewing, so it stays clear of the gameplay-client line.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: speak Magic, not Forge (units, costs, names)
patterns.seen_in: Sim Lab shows 'T36' next to 'won on round 10', 'median death turn T36', 'Assembled 1 of 8 (T57)', mana costs as raw '{1}{G}{G}{G}' on /decks, and log lines 'Forest - {T}: Add {G}.'. NN/g heuristic #2.
patterns.why_it_works: In Commander talk, 'turn 6' means everyone's sixth turn, the same thing Sim Lab calls a 'round'. Forge's global turn counter (T36) is engine-speak that no player uses, and showing both forces every reader to do arithmetic.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Use one unit everywhere: call rounds 'turn N' in UI copy (with a single glossary line), and never display Forge's global counter. Render mana costs with the commissioned painted pips at 14 to 16px, which are IP-safe and already exist, or as tight glyph clusters. Never show raw braces outside verbatim oracle text. Use a true minus (−16.1), an en dash for empty values, and 'n/a' only where a value cannot exist.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: a combo is what it produces; group, classify, collapse
patterns.seen_in: Commander Spellbook shows each combo's results ('Infinite colorless mana', 'Infinite storm count') and folds variants. The Sim Lab Win conditions table lists 38 rows, including 28 Squirrel Girl variants, 'Stella Lee, Wild Card' (the commander alone), and 'Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring … AI can fire this; results meaningful'.
patterns.why_it_works: The playtester called it baffling because the label is false: none of these win alone. Collapsing identical structure is Tufte's 'erase redundant data-ink', and classifying by outcome matches how players think about combos (win versus engine).
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Group per deck into three bands. 'Wins on its own' covers results that include win the game, infinite damage or each opponent loses. 'Engine' covers infinite mana, storm or ETBs, and names the payoff cards present in the deck. 'Not a combo' covers single cards and the commander alone, which should be hidden. Fold variants under the shared core ('Squirrel Girl + Concordant Crossroads + one of 7 haste or token pieces'). Show assembled and one-card-away rows first; put the rest behind 'n more'. Replace the per-row 'too few games to measure this' with one sentence above the table. Fit the table to the column width so 'Piece most often missing' is never clipped.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: every number answers 'compared to what?' and carries its uncertainty visually, once
patterns.seen_in: Tufte (graphical integrity). Sim Lab's prediction block (range and ±4.0 stated, which is good). The scorecards show '57% (4 of 7)' with no interval, and the telemetry page shows 'Charge counters 0.12/g · Partial' for a reanimator deck.
patterns.why_it_works: Seven decided games cannot distinguish 57% from 30% (a Wilson interval of roughly 25 to 84%). Printing it bare, or printing irrelevant metrics precisely, is fake precision. Showing the interval is more honest and more expert.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Win-rate bars get an interval whisker and the 25% pod baseline as a tick (the tick exists; add the whisker). Rows with n<10 render in --ink-3 with a single top-of-section note ('8 games is a sniff test; about 32 to compare decks'). Blocking and attacking figures become a compact table with a 'table average' column beside each deck figure, so '15% blocked' means something. Telemetry must say 'We don't know this deck's plan yet' rather than scoring a default archetype's counters.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: one sentence, then the evidence; delete anything that restates it
patterns.seen_in: design_principles.md (prose opener) and Stripe's 'lead with a sentence'. Sim Lab results page: the opener gives 8 games, 50%, 1 draw and 12 rounds, and the 4-figure strip directly under it repeats all four.
patterns.why_it_works: Redundant restatement is filler generators produce to 'fill the layout'. People notice they have read the same thing twice, and it lowers trust in the rest.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Delete the results-page figure strip, or make it carry what the sentence does not (for example the pod's median elimination turn and the game length spread). Apply one test to every screen: if deleting an element loses no information, delete it (law 5, 'fixes subtract').

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: judgment over rules for states the system knows are broken
patterns.seen_in: Coaching page: a glowing primary 'GENERATE COACHING REPORT (~$0.01, ABOUT 20 S)' plus 'the button above will fail. Set MTG_LLM_API_KEY in deploy/.env and redeploy'. /results/[file] shows 'NaN:NaN' duration and 'Draw (draw)'.
patterns.why_it_works: 'Never disable the primary' exists so users know what blocks them, not to promote a button that cannot work. Operator instructions shown to players are the clearest sign that nobody looked at the screen as a user.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: When a feature is dark, the page says so in player language ('Coaching is not switched on yet') with no primary, and the operator detail moves to deploy/preflight.py output. Add formatter guards: a missing duration renders '–', and an outcome label never repeats its category. Add a check to .claude/skills/ui-review: 'no NaN, undefined, raw ids, braces or env var names in rendered text'.

patterns.pattern: ADOPT: finish the furniture (the small details real products have)
patterns.seen_in: Rams ('thorough down to the last detail'). design_principles.md Part 3 #10. Sim Lab gaps: every tab titled 'Arcane Sim Lab'; prediction headers centred over left-aligned numbers; an 8-row games table with a search box; the home cost hint in 11px mono reading like debug output.
patterns.why_it_works: People judge craft by the absence of small failures more than by the presence of flourishes. Aligned numerals, correct titles and proportionate controls signal that someone checked.
patterns.apply_to_simlab: Give each page a real <title> ('Kess vs Stella Lee vs … · Game 1 · Sim Lab'). Right-align numeric columns with right-aligned headers. Show filters only when a list exceeds about 20 rows. Set the duration hint as normal UI text beside the primary. Add hover-to-preview on every card name in the event log and tables, as Moxfield does.

research.summary:
Verdict: Sim Lab's jank is mostly not a lack of polish. Its binding visual spec builds in the look people now recognise as AI-made, and the data surfaces leak engine output and untested edge cases.

The home page is exactly what DESIGN_SYSTEM.md §5/§6 prescribes, and it is the most recognisable AI landing composition there is: a centred mascot over the wordmark on purple and cyan storm art, a four-tile vanity stat strip, the chatbot prompt 'What would you like to do today?', and four equal uppercase glowing CTA tiles that repeat the nav. On top of that, the body font is Space Grotesk, which Anthropic's own frontend-design prompt names as the face models converge on. The repo's earlier research (mockups/design_principles.md Part 1) listed glassmorphism, glows, stat banners, all-caps labels, Space Grotesk and the centred hero as AI tells, and the Arcane reskin adopted five of them. A blind study (arXiv 2605.15124, n=92) found AI-built UIs score fine on usability and poorly on originality. That is the owner's complaint.

The deeper 'nobody looked' signals are specific and fixable:
- **Names:** truncated run and seat names ('Kess, vs Stella vs Skrat's vs Krenko', 'revenge's untap').
- **Results page:** 'NaN:NaN' and 'Draw (draw)' in the games table; Forge's global turn counter (T36, T57) shown next to 'round 10'.
- **Replay log:** raw Forge output, including '(995)' ids, 'Forest - {T}: Add {G}.', reminder text as events, '[Card: … SpellAbility: …]' and every step of every turn.
- **Win conditions:** 28 Squirrel Girl variants, the commander listed as a combo, and Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring called a win.
- **Telemetry:** Kess Reanimator scored on 'Charge counters 0.12/g'.
- **Coaching:** a glowing primary that the page says will fail, next to deploy instructions.
- **Replay board:** cards measured at 28x40px and 44x62px on a 1440px screen, with the transport below the fold at 1440x900.

The strengths are real and worth protecting: prose openers, the calibrated voice of 'Against real playgroups' (range, ±4.0, 'read the ranking first'), seat rotation with the 25% marker, same-scale scorecards, the replay's keyboard transport, deep links and 'jump to the deciding turn', the /new commander-art deck picker, the a11y contract, the IP-safe painted pips, and the em-dash rule.

Principles a developer can apply to every future screen:
1. **Name it like a player.** Use commander names and art for decks, 'turn N' as players count it, and combos by what they produce (Commander Spellbook's results). Never show an engine token, filename, instance id, env var or raw {cost} braces.
2. **Every number answers 'compared to what, out of how many?'** Put the baseline, n and an interval beside every rate. When n is too small, say it once and dim the figure instead of printing it confidently. Never score a plan you have not identified.
3. **Show the game, not the log.** A replay starts with an overview: a life chart per seat that doubles as the scrubber, plus key moments. Then a legible board that fits the viewport (battlefield cards about 96px wide, lands collapsed, eliminated seats greyed). The full log is one toggle away, filtered to actions, with repeated lines collapsed. Viewing only: no stops, no adjudication.
4. **Art is a stage; data is paper.** Keep fantasy art where nothing is read (the home masthead, empty states) and put content on an opaque ground (Apple HIG: no glass in the content layer). Glow means live, and nothing else glows.
5. **One sentence, then the evidence.** Open with computed prose and delete any element that repeats it ('fixes subtract').
6. **Collapse what is the same.** Fold variants, repeated step lines and 'didn't block' runs into one line with a count. Show only what is assembled or one card away by default.
7. **Judgment over rules.** A design-system rule never justifies a broken state. A dark feature says so plainly with no primary, and operator detail never reaches players.
8. **Details are the brand.** No NaN or dangling commas, no clipped columns, a real per-page title, right-aligned tabular figures, a true minus, sentence-case buttons, and hover previews on every card name. People take the absence of these failures as proof of care.
9. **Choose, don't converge.** Every type, colour and layout choice needs a reason tied to Commander players (for example, a body face picked for dense card names and tabular figures instead of Space Grotesk). If a choice matches what a generator would produce with no brief, make it again.

Spec changes to propose to the owner:
- **Remove:** DESIGN_SYSTEM §5's home order, §6's tally banner and action hub, glass behind data, and the Space Grotesk body face.
- **Keep:** the a11y contract, status shapes (and stop reusing them for game outcomes), the pips, the em-dash rule, and law 5.
